The COVID-19 Pandemic. In late 2019, a novel coronavirus emerged in Wuhan, China. Named SARS-CoV-2, it likely originated from animal-to-human transmission, though the exact initial spillover route remains debated. From that beginning, the virus spread globally, killing an estimated 7 to 20 million people by 2024.

The virus spreads through respiratory droplets and aerosol transmission. Severity ranged from asymptomatic infection to severe pneumonia and multi-organ failure, particularly in elderly and immunocompromised populations. The actual death toll is likely far higher than official reports, due to underreporting in many countries.

The pandemic prompted unprecedented international lockdowns, border closures, school shutdowns, and business closures. These measures disrupted economies worldwide and created secondary health crises in mental health and routine medical care. Global responses achieved something remarkable: vaccines developed in under a year using mRNA technology from Pfizer and Moderna, and viral-vector approaches began rollout in late 2020. These vaccines saved millions of lives, though their distribution was deeply inequitable globally.

The pandemic exposed weak global health governance, supply chain fragility, and stark disparities. Wealthy nations hoarded vaccines while poor nations faced shortages. The virus continued as endemic circulation, with new variants including Delta and Omicron emerging and surging. In vaccinated populations, the disease burden shifted toward respiratory symptoms and became less lethal but remained highly transmissible.
